title: Lecture 5 - Randomized Algorithms MCQs
description: Midterm MCQs on concepts, mathematical reasoning and proof steps. No code tracing or code-analysis questions.
subject: Algorithm Analysis

questions.question: Why can randomized pivoting help quicksort on a fixed sorted input of distinct keys?
options: Sorted inputs cease to contain n elements.
Partitioning becomes constant time.
Every chosen pivot is guaranteed to be the exact median.
Input order no longer determines a fixed bad pivot sequence.
questions.correctAnswer: Input order no longer determines a fixed bad pivot sequence.
questions.explanation: Random pivot choices remove the systematic first/last-pivot bias without guaranteeing every split is good.

questions.question: Which description matches a Las Vegas algorithm?
options: It can return wrong answers but always uses exactly one operation.
It returns correct answers, while its runtime depends on random choices.
Its runtime is necessarily constant.
It never uses randomness.
questions.correctAnswer: It returns correct answers, while its runtime depends on random choices.
questions.explanation: Correctness is preserved; the random quantity is computational effort.

questions.question: Which description matches a Monte Carlo algorithm?
options: Its only uncertainty is the programmer's identity.
It must sort an array.
It is always correct and never has a runtime bound.
Its work is bounded, but its answer can have a controlled probability of error.
questions.correctAnswer: Its work is bounded, but its answer can have a controlled probability of error.
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo algorithms permit error probability, unlike the lecture's Las Vegas examples.

questions.question: How are randomized quicksort and randomized quickselect classified in this lecture?
options: Monte Carlo because random pivots can produce wrong answers.
Approximation algorithms that always return nearly correct ranks.
Las Vegas.
Deterministic because their input is fixed.
questions.correctAnswer: Las Vegas.
questions.explanation: Correctly implemented pivot choices change runtime, not the required result.

questions.question: What is the main performance metric for a Las Vegas algorithm?
options: Expected running time.
Only the number of source files.
Probability that a correct implementation returns a wrong answer.
The color of its output.
questions.correctAnswer: Expected running time.
questions.explanation: The runtime varies over the random choices, while output correctness is maintained.

questions.question: Which qualification matters when claiming repetition reduces Monte Carlo error?
options: Reusing exactly the same random choices always gives independent trials.
The trials and output-combination rule must support the claimed reduction.
Repeating a wrong answer guarantees correctness.
A Monte Carlo algorithm becomes deterministic after two runs.
questions.correctAnswer: The trials and output-combination rule must support the claimed reduction.
questions.explanation: Independent trials with an appropriate decision rule can reduce error; repetition alone is not a universal guarantee.

questions.question: What is the expected running time of standard randomized quicksort on distinct keys with uniform pivots?
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(log n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.correctAnswer: Θ(n log n)
questions.explanation: Averaging over random pivots gives linearithmic expected work for any fixed order of distinct keys.

questions.question: Does uniform random pivoting remove quicksort's theoretical quadratic worst case?
options: No; sufficiently unlucky pivot sequences can still give Θ(n²).
Yes; every run is guaranteed Θ(n log n).
Yes; every split becomes exactly equal.
No; its expected time also necessarily becomes Θ(n²).
questions.correctAnswer: No; sufficiently unlucky pivot sequences can still give Θ(n²).
questions.explanation: Expected performance improves, but the worst possible random sequence remains quadratic.

questions.question: Which pivot sequence causes quicksort's worst-case shape on distinct keys?
options: Always producing two equal-size sides.
Always choosing a middle-ranked key.
Choosing each rank once after sorting is already complete.
Repeatedly choosing the smallest or largest remaining key.
questions.correctAnswer: Repeatedly choosing the smallest or largest remaining key.
questions.explanation: An extreme pivot leaves a side of size n-1 at each step.

questions.question: Which recurrence models consistently balanced quicksort with linear partition work?
questions.explanation: Quicksort sorts both roughly equal sides after partitioning.

questions.question: Which statement about median-of-three quicksort pivoting is correct?
options: It guarantees constant-time sorting.
It removes the partition step.
It always finds the exact global median.
It can help in practice but still has quadratic worst cases.
questions.correctAnswer: It can help in practice but still has quadratic worst cases.
questions.explanation: A small deterministic sample is a heuristic, not a universal balanced-split guarantee.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] For distinct ranked keys zᵢ and zⱼ, i<j, how many ranks lie in the inclusive interval i through j?
options: j+i
j-i-1
j-i+1
j-i
questions.correctAnswer: j-i+1
questions.explanation: The inclusive interval contains both endpoints plus its interior ranks.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] In randomized quicksort on distinct keys, when are zᵢ and zⱼ directly compared?
options: Only after both keys have been removed from all subproblems.
When the first pivot from that interval is strictly between them.
When the first pivot from ranks i through j is either endpoint.
Only when every pivot is a median.
questions.correctAnswer: When the first pivot from ranks i through j is either endpoint.
questions.explanation: An endpoint pivot compares them; an interior pivot separates them before a direct comparison.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] For distinct keys and uniform pivots, what is P(zᵢ and zⱼ are compared), i<j?
questions.explanation: Two favorable endpoint ranks are among j-i+1 equally likely first pivots in the interval.

questions.question: What is the comparison probability for adjacent ranks in randomized quicksort on distinct keys?
options: 1/n²
2/n for every n
questions.explanation: For j=i+1, the formula is 2/(j-i+1)=2/2=1.

questions.question: For n distinct keys, what is the probability that the minimum and maximum are directly compared?
options: 1/n²
questions.explanation: They are compared only if an endpoint is the first pivot among all n ranks.

questions.question: What is the comparison probability for ranks 2 and 6 under uniform randomized quicksort on distinct keys?
questions.explanation: The inclusive interval has 6-2+1=5 ranks, with two favorable endpoints.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] If Xᵢⱼ indicates whether each unordered pair is compared, which expectation formula counts comparisons once?
options: E[C]=2Σ(i<j) P(Xᵢⱼ=1), even after the probability includes both endpoints.
E[C]=the product of all pair probabilities.
E[C]=the probability of comparing just the minimum and maximum.
E[C]=Σ(i<j) E[Xᵢⱼ]=Σ(i<j) P(Xᵢⱼ=1)
questions.correctAnswer: E[C]=Σ(i<j) E[Xᵢⱼ]=Σ(i<j) P(Xᵢⱼ=1)
questions.explanation: C is the sum of pair indicators. Linearity gives the sum of probabilities without another factor of two.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] Does linearity of expectation require the pair-comparison indicators to be independent?
options: No; because the indicators are always all equal.
No; expectation of a sum is the sum of expectations even without independence.
Yes; otherwise expectations are undefined.
Yes; every pair must be independent of every other pair.
questions.correctAnswer: No; expectation of a sum is the sum of expectations even without independence.
questions.explanation: Independence is unnecessary for linearity; it is a different requirement used in other probability rules.

questions.question: What problem does quickselect solve?
options: Sort both partitions completely on every call.
Compute a matrix product.
Find only the maximum regardless of k.
Find a requested k-th smallest element without fully sorting every side.
questions.correctAnswer: Find a requested k-th smallest element without fully sorting every side.
questions.explanation: Selection requires an order statistic, not the complete sorted ordering.

questions.question: After partitioning in quickselect, where does recursion continue if the pivot is not the target?
options: In both sides, exactly as in quicksort.
Only in the side containing the desired rank.
Only in the side not containing the target.
In neither side for every target.
questions.correctAnswer: Only in the side containing the desired rank.
questions.explanation: The pivot rank identifies the one side that can contain the requested order statistic.

questions.question: [Proof MCQ] Why does the balanced quickselect recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(n) give Θ(n)?
options: The work n+n/2+n/4+... is a geometric series of order n.
There are n levels each costing n.
Both sides must be added at every level.
Every call has zero partition cost.
questions.correctAnswer: The work n+n/2+n/4+... is a geometric series of order n.
questions.explanation: One retained branch means level costs shrink geometrically rather than remaining n across a full branching tree.

questions.question: Under uniform pivots on distinct keys, which pairing describes randomized quickselect?
options: Θ(log n) expected time and Θ(1) worst-case time.
Θ(n²) expected time and Θ(n) worst-case time.
Θ(n log n) expected time and Θ(n log n) worst-case time.
Θ(n) expected time and Θ(n²) worst-case time.
questions.correctAnswer: Θ(n) expected time and Θ(n²) worst-case time.
questions.explanation: Only one relevant partition is explored; expectation is linear, but repeated poor shrinkage can still be quadratic.

questions.question: Using the lecture's 0-based global target-index convention, what index represents the fourth smallest element?
options: k=n-4 for every input size
questions.explanation: The first smallest is index 0, so the fourth is index 3; a 1-based rank convention would use 4.

questions.question: Why is a three-way partition useful when many keys equal the pivot?
options: It changes Las Vegas selection into a possibly wrong Monte Carlo method.
It groups equal keys together so repeated equal values need not form a long chain of nearly unchanged subproblems.
It removes the need to specify the target rank.
It guarantees every pivot has a unique value.
questions.correctAnswer: It groups equal keys together so repeated equal values need not form a long chain of nearly unchanged subproblems.
questions.explanation: The equal-to-pivot group can be handled at once; simple two-way schemes can degrade with heavy duplication.
